A Republican campaign mailer in Connecticut depicting Democratic state Rep. Matthew Lesser — who is Jewish — as a money-grubbing caricature has drawn widespread condemnation as anti‑Semitic. The full‑color, double‑sided piece, sent by GOP state Senate candidate Ed Charamut in the Middletown-area district, used an altered photograph of Lesser with exaggerated eyes and hands clutching $100 bills alongside the tagline “Matt Lesser will take everything you worked for.” Critics said the imagery invoked an age-old anti‑Jewish trope.

Lesser and Jewish leaders reacted with shock and outrage, noting the mailer arrived shortly after the Pittsburgh synagogue massacre and saying the image revived longstanding stereotypes. The Connecticut Anti‑Defamation League and scholars called the ad “reprehensible” and “deeply offensive.” Media commentators and others framed the mailer in the context of heightened concerns about rising anti‑Semitism and racially charged political advertising nationally.

Allan Greenspan, Charamut’s Jewish campaign treasurer, acknowledged the candidate’s eyes were altered to look “bigger and greedy,” and Charamut initially defended the piece as commentary on tax policy, denying hateful intent. After mounting criticism, Charamut’s campaign apologized, saying the imagery could be interpreted as anti‑Semitic and expressing regret; the state GOP chair also reversed course, acknowledged the ad’s offensive undertones, said the party had not approved it, and said he would meet with the ADL to learn more.

The episode prompted broader discussion of divisive campaign tactics and the role of national rhetoric in emboldening bigotry, with Democrats blaming President Trump’s rhetoric for fostering an environment that tolerates such attacks.

A group of six women Greenpeace activists climbed the Shard in London on 11 July 2013 to protest Shell’s Arctic drilling. Starting in the early hours after gaining access from the roof of London Bridge station, they used a mix of rope-access, traditional climbing and sections of free-climbing on the Shard’s external metal frame. After a 16‑hour ascent they reached the 310 m summit, unfurled “Save the Arctic” flags and displayed large artwork aimed at drawing attention to Arctic oil and gas development. Greenpeace named the climbers and livestreamed parts of the action; the charity said the location was chosen because the Shard is near Shell’s London offices and resembles a shard of ice.

The Met Police arrested all six on suspicion of aggravated trespass. The Shard’s viewing platform was temporarily closed for safety; building management and emergency teams worked with authorities to protect protesters, staff and the public. Greenpeace framed the action as part of a global campaign against Arctic drilling; Shell said it respected free expression, defended responsible Arctic operations and emphasised its experience and safety work in the region. Observers noted the climb used standard industrial-access equipment and involved significant risk but followed techniques common to building access workers.

Knightscope’s security robots (notably the 300-pound, five-foot-tall K5) can perform thermal imaging to monitor critical equipment temperatures, trigger alerts at set thresholds, capture data for historical analysis/pattern recognition, and detect fires. The company markets these robots for crime prevention and surveillance—equipped with 360° video and license-plate reading capabilities—and leases them to clients.

News coverage focused on a recent Mountain View incident: on April 19 a reportedly intoxicated 41-year-old man, Jason Sylvain, allegedly knocked a Knightscope K5 over while it was patrolling a company parking lot. The robot sounded alarms and the suspect fled but was detained by employees and arrested by police on charges including prowling and public intoxication. Knightscope said the robot detected the assault, sounded alarms, and sustained only scratches before returning to patrol. The episode recalled prior incidents (including a K5 running over a toddler’s foot last year) and prompted public discussion about how people and robots interact, whether laws or behavioral changes are needed, and how robots should be programmed to handle human interference.

A new USGS-led study of a previously underexamined ~100-mile stretch of the San Andreas Fault — from the Antelope Valley through the Grapevine/Tejon Pass area near Frazier Park — finds that large earthquakes have occurred there roughly every 100 years. By identifying ten prehistoric events over the past ~1,200 years, researchers conclude this segment is about 160 years past its average recurrence interval and is therefore overdue for a major quake. Most of the identified events were magnitude ~7.5 or larger, which could cause widespread disruption (for example to power and to Interstate 5 access into Los Angeles). Scientists emphasize the findings are not a reason to panic but to reinforce preparedness for a large earthquake on this part of the fault. (The document also briefly mentions internet-archiving efforts aimed at preventing broken links.)

Kellogg Co. announced it is halting operations in Venezuela, citing the country’s severe economic and social deterioration. The plant employed about 400 workers and produced most locally consumed breakfast cereal. The company said it had written off its Venezuela assets and warned it is not responsible for any unauthorized use of its brands.

President Nicolás Maduro moved quickly to seize Kellogg’s local units and said they would be handed over to workers; he also announced judicial proceedings against the company, calling the exit unconstitutional. The takeover follows a pattern in Venezuela where the government has seized or nationalized facilities after multinational withdrawals (e.g., Kimberly‑Clark, Clorox). Maduro blames the crisis on an “economic war” by foreign and domestic actors.

Companies operating in Venezuela have struggled with hyperinflation, strict currency controls that limit imports, shortages of raw materials, and government price controls that often force sales below cost. Several multinationals — including General Mills, Procter & Gamble, Clorox, Kimberly‑Clark and others — have scaled back, exited or had assets expropriated amid the country’s shortages and protests. Kellogg said it hopes to return in the future but warned it will pursue legal action to protect its trademarks and assets.

Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir, wanted by the International Criminal Court on genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity charges over atrocities in Darfur, left South Africa on June 15–16 while a Pretoria court was considering an application to order his arrest. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre and other rights groups had sought enforcement of ICC arrest warrants from 2009 and 2010; a South African judge had ordered al-Bashir to remain in the country and instructed ports to bar his exit. Despite that order, al-Bashir’s plane was moved from Johannesburg’s Tambo Airport to the Waterkloof military air base and he departed for Khartoum before the detention ruling was finalized. South African and Sudanese officials confirmed his return; Sudan welcomed him with public celebrations.

The incident sparked domestic and international criticism. Rights groups and opposition politicians accused the South African government of flouting the rule of law and failing to execute its obligations as a Rome Statute signatory. The U.N., ICC officials and some foreign governments said South Africa must comply with its treaty duties, while some African leaders and South African ruling-party figures argued the ICC disproportionately targets Africans and defended allowing al-Bashir’s summit attendance. The episode renewed scrutiny of the ICC’s effectiveness and political pressures facing states asked to arrest powerful sitting leaders. The Darfur conflict, which led to the charges, has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions since 2003.

Budweiser’s Super Bowl commercial "Brotherhood" — about a man who raises a baby Clydesdale and later reunites with it, set to Fleetwood Mac’s “Landslide” — has become the No. 3 most‑shared Super Bowl ad ever, according to Unruly. By Monday it had more than 1.5 million shares (mostly on Facebook), trailing Volkswagen’s 2011 "The Force" (5.5M) and Budweiser’s own "9/11" spot (2.3M). The foal, born Jan. 16, was the subject of Budweiser’s first tweet asking fans to name it; Bud’s Facebook post of the ad received 19,000+ likes and 16,000+ shares. The spot ranks No. 24 on the list of most‑shared ads overall.

The write‑up also highlights other standout Super Bowl ads: a late‑game Dodge commercial that used Paul Harvey’s 1978 “So God Made a Farmer” speech over farm images, noted for its emotional impact (and similarity to a 2011 Farms.com YouTube video). It concludes that many Super Bowl spots feel less remarkable now because high‑quality content appears daily online.

Separately, Coca‑Cola’s second‑consecutive integrated TV+online campaign, "Coke Chase," had mixed results. The interactive race site drew 1.3 million visitors, 910,000 votes and 7.3 million “sabotages,” but overall participation was lower than Coke’s 2012 polar‑bear live feed (about 9 million check‑ins). Technical glitches during the game hindered functionality for some users. Still, Coke’s 60‑second Coke Chase spot has been viewed 2.5 million times, outpacing the 1.7 million combined views of the 2012 polar‑bear videos.

The Millennium Tower, a 58-story luxury condominium in downtown San Francisco completed in 2009, has become a focal point of public concern, legal battles and engineering debate after it was discovered to be sinking and tilting. Owner and resident accounts, investigative reporting (including a 60 Minutes segment), satellite data and engineering studies show the building has settled roughly 17 inches since construction began and leans about 14 inches toward the northwest. Residents report widening cracks in basement columns, stress gauges monitoring movement, and dramatic everyday effects (e.g., marbles rolling on tilted floors). Some owners have sold at steep losses and others fear seismic safety, though city reviews to date have concluded the tower still meets performance-based seismic criteria.

The root of the problem is contested. Millennium Partners and some owners blame nearby construction—especially the Transbay Transit Center project—for destabilizing soil by groundwater pumping. Independent Bay Area geotechnical engineers and critics point to a different, central issue: the tower’s 900 concrete piles extend only 60–91 feet into dense sand and rubble rather than down to bedrock about 200 feet below, and the heavy concrete structure was not anchored to bedrock as many argue it should have been. That combination of heavy weight and non-uniform settlement into bay fill and historic landfill is consistent with ongoing sinking and tilting.

There are many parties involved in litigation—developers, engineers, the Transbay authority, contractors, the homeowners association, the city and high-profile owners—and mediation is ongoing. Proposed technical remedies under study include installing 50–100 new large-diameter piles drilled from the basement down to bedrock (estimated cost roughly $100–150 million), which engineers say could stabilize and re-level the building while residents might be allowed to stay during work. Other proposed, less practical options discussed publicly included freezing the ground or removing upper stories.

The controversy has prompted the city to tighten review of high-rise foundation designs (though bedrock anchoring is not universally required) and triggered reassessments for some owners’ property taxes. Responsibility for costs remains unresolved and will likely be litigated, but officials and many stakeholders express the priority should be to implement a fix quickly and settle financial and legal disputes afterward.

Abdul Qadeer Khan, the founder of Pakistan’s nuclear weapons program, provided documents — including a July 15, 1998 letter he says was written by North Korean Workers’ Party Secretary Jon Byong Ho — claiming North Korea paid more than $3 million in kickbacks to senior Pakistani military officers in exchange for nuclear-related technology and components in the late 1990s. Khan says he personally delivered payments totaling about $3 million (plus an earlier $0.5 million and gifts) to two generals; the North Korean letter, marked “Secret,” requests that “agreed documents, components, etc.” be loaded on a North Korean plane after missile deliveries.

The materials were given to Simon Henderson of the Washington Institute for Near East Policy and shared with Western media. Some U.S. and IAEA-related experts told The Washington Post the letter’s details and signature appear authentic and fit known facts about Pakistan’s assistance to North Korea (including centrifuge designs similar to the P2 model Khan trafficked). Other analysts find the account plausible given later North Korean uranium-enrichment developments observed at Yongbyon.

Pakistani officials named in the accusations — retired generals Jehangir Karamat and Zulfiqar Khan — and Pakistani government sources have strongly denied the claims, calling the letter a fabrication and arguing Khan is trying to shift blame for his illicit proliferation activities. Pakistani probes and a prior U.S. inquiry produced inconclusive results, in part because U.S. investigators were restricted from questioning Khan. Khan’s credibility is contested domestically: some hail him as a hero while others accuse him of profiting personally and acting without official sanction.

If genuine, the letter would be a striking instance of corruption linking Pakistan’s military to illicit technology transfers that helped North Korea pursue a uranium-based bomb route. However, independent verification remains lacking, and experts remain divided over whether the documents prove high-level complicity or merely Khan’s assertions of wider involvement.

A new Commonwealth Fund report comparing 11 high-income countries finds the United States ranks last overall in health system performance despite spending far more per person than any peer. The study evaluated access, quality, efficiency and equity across Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland, the U.K., and the U.S. The U.K.’s single-payer system ranked first; Switzerland placed second.

Key findings:
- The U.S. spends the most per capita ($8,508) but performs worse than most peers on outcomes, access, efficiency and equity.
- Major U.S. shortcomings include limited access to primary care (especially for low-income groups), a shortage of primary care physicians, high out-of-pocket barriers that lead people to skip care or prescriptions, high infant mortality, excess deaths from controllable conditions (e.g., hypertension), and lower healthy life expectancy at older ages.
- U.S. physicians struggle with care coordination, timely information exchange and administrative burdens, though preventive and patient-centered care areas score relatively well.
- The data were collected prior to full implementation of the Affordable Care Act, so expanded coverage from the ACA could improve future rankings, but authors say deeper reforms in accountability, information systems and incentives will be needed to close gaps.

Analysts note that countries that improved their rankings (e.g., the U.K.) did so through systematic reforms: increasing resources, boosting primary and specialist capacity, rewarding quality, and adopting health information systems. The report’s lead author emphasizes the need for accountability and broad professional buy-in to achieve meaningful improvement in U.S. health system performance.

A 1-year-old girl, Katera Barker, died after being accidentally left in a pickup truck in East Nashville on May 23, 2018. Her father, Matt Barker, dropped the couple’s 5-year-old at daycare around 7:30 a.m. and unintentionally left Katera in her rear-facing car seat in the truck. He returned home briefly, then left by rideshare for a business flight. The mother, Jenny Barker, drove to work thinking both children were at daycare; she only discovered that Katera had not been dropped off when she went to pick up the children that evening. She called her husband, returned home, found Katera in the vehicle around 5:30–5:42 p.m., performed CPR until paramedics arrived, and the child was pronounced dead at Vanderbilt Children’s Hospital.

Temperatures that day were in the upper 80s and interior vehicle heat can rise rapidly—often reaching life-threatening levels in an hour—so the truck’s interior likely exceeded 100°F. Police say the parents are cooperating with an ongoing investigation and no charges have been filed. The death is at least the seventh hot-car child fatality in the U.S. so far that year; NoHeatStroke.org reports 749 vehicular heatstroke deaths of children since 1998.

Authorities and safety advocates recommend simple memory aids to prevent such tragedies, such as placing a purse, shoe, stuffed animal, phone, or other essential item in the back seat with the child so caregivers must check the rear before leaving the vehicle. Tennessee law protects some Good Samaritans who rescue children from locked cars, but requires callers to notify 911 or law enforcement before forcing entry.

A disruptive passenger aboard United Flight 116 from Hong Kong to Newark was restrained by fellow travelers and taken into custody and hospitalized after demanding the plane be diverted to Canada and ranting about the CIA, Edward Snowden and being targeted.

Passengers said the man, identified by officials as Daniel Morgan Perry and reportedly an American in his 30s, became loud and paranoid about nine hours into the roughly 15–16 hour flight, accusing others of working for U.S. intelligence, saying he was being poisoned and repeatedly proclaiming “I’m dead.” Several passengers and a flight attendant subdued him with plastic restraints supplied by the crew; there were no air marshals on board. He was escorted off the plane by FBI agents when it landed at Newark Liberty International Airport and taken to University Hospital for observation. United said it followed procedures and completed the flight as scheduled. Passengers who sat with him afterward said he appeared unstable, responded to calming conversation, and at one point asked to be arrested, saying he didn’t want to frighten children. The FBI has been working to clarify his statements.

Over the past ten days Donald Trump’s standing has declined sharply across key swing states, erasing gains Republicans had hoped would carry into Election Day and putting their prospects for holding Congress at risk. Public polls show Trump trailing in Pennsylvania and slipping in Florida and North Carolina; private polling indicates even larger losses among independents, moderate Republicans and women. Republican leaders who had softened criticism now face urgent decisions about whether to distance themselves from Trump, possibly as soon as after Sunday’s debate.

Trump has shifted his electoral hopes westward—campaigning in Colorado, Arizona and Nevada—seeking a narrow path to 270 electoral votes similar to past Republican strategies. But Clinton’s strong first-debate performance and Trump’s post-debate missteps have made Western states more competitive than anticipated. In Colorado, post-debate polls show Clinton leading by double digits in some measures, and suburban women and growing Hispanic and millennial populations remain key to victory. Arizona and Nevada have tightened, with Nevada polls showing Clinton ahead by 1–6 points; Trump’s appeal to white men and some union voters gives him limited upside there, but his volatility and weak standing with Hispanics remain liabilities.

Third-party candidate Gary Johnson, who polls near double digits in some Western states, complicates the map by drawing younger and anti-establishment voters from both parties. Clinton’s campaign benefits from stronger organization and turnout potential among the Obama coalition, though Democrats worry about lukewarm enthusiasm among millennials, Hispanics and African-Americans. Overall, unless Trump substantially improves his debate performances and campaign execution, he may no longer control his electoral destiny, with Western battlegrounds and turnout dynamics likely to determine the race.

Researchers at Binghamton University showed that brief EEG responses to words can serve as a stable biometric “brainprint.” In the study, 45 volunteers read 75 acronyms while EEG was recorded from only three scalp electrodes. Machine-learning classifiers could identify individuals from their event‑related potentials (ERPs) with very high accuracy (reported in the paper and media summaries as roughly 82–97%, typically cited around 94%). These distinguishing ERP features were stable over time—identification remained possible after delays up to six months. 

The team emphasizes potential advantages of brain biometrics over fingerprints or retinal scans: they may be cancellable (users could change the stimuli that produce the signature) and harder to spoof or permanently compromise. The authors see near‑term application mainly in high‑security settings (e.g., military or sensitive facilities) rather than casual consumer login, given the need to record EEG. The study appears in Neurocomputing and was supported by NSF and Binghamton University grants.

This mixed report combines two news stories: an interview about Dylann Roof, the suspect in the Charleston, South Carolina church massacre, and extended coverage of the Ferguson, Missouri protests after the shooting of Michael Brown.

Dylann Roof
- Dylann Roof, 21, was arrested on suspicion of killing nine people at a historic African-American church in South Carolina.
- Family members describe Roof as withdrawn and troubled. An uncle said Roof spent long periods alone in his room, lacked a job and driver's license, and resisted mentoring.
- The uncle and other available online images suggested Roof had a fascination with white supremacy.
- The uncle also said Roof’s father bought him a pistol for his birthday earlier in the year.
- Reporting was incomplete at the time; more information was promised.

Ferguson and Michael Brown
- Authorities identified the officer who shot Michael Brown as 28-year-old Darren Wilson, a six-year police veteran. Police had earlier withheld his name citing threats.
- Ferguson Police Chief Thomas Jackson described Wilson as a “gentleman” and defended him, saying the situation was devastating for the officer.
- Police released a convenience-store surveillance video and documents showing a strong, larger man (police say appears to be Brown) leaving a store with a box of cigars without paying; authorities listed Brown as the “primary suspect” in that incident. The chief said the robbery did not relate to the initial police contact, though he suggested the officer might have seen evidence connected to it.
- The release of the video and documents on the same day as naming the officer stirred controversy; Brown’s family and supporters said the distribution amounted to a smear and a diversion from the shooting itself.
- Witnesses offered conflicting accounts of the shooting: some say Brown had his hands up when shot; others described a struggle over the officer’s gun and pursuit. A companion, Dorian Johnson, called Brown’s death murder.
- The release of the robbery details and the handling of information by police intensified distrust and protests in Ferguson. Critics accused authorities of mismanaging the situation and of a heavy-handed, militarized response to demonstrations; some protesters engaged in clashes and looting earlier in the week.
- After the Missouri State Highway Patrol assumed security, demonstrations were more peaceful. Capt. Ron Johnson, who led the patrol’s response, emphasized transparency, urged calm, and suggested the episode would spark national discussion about police tactics and diversity training.
- Local activists, civil-rights leaders and Brown’s family planned further rallies demanding action; the prospect of criminal charges against Officer Wilson remained a possibility.

Overall themes
- The document highlights two racially charged acts of violence and their social fallout: the Charleston church massacre linked to alleged white supremacist interest, and the contentious police shooting of Michael Brown that prompted protests, debate over police transparency, and scrutiny of law-enforcement tactics.

Archaeological investigations at the Nazi death camp Treblinka, presented in the Smithsonian Channel documentary "Treblinka: Hitler’s Killing Machine," have uncovered new physical evidence confirming mass graves and the presence of gas chambers at the site. Forensic archaeologist Dr. Caroline Sturdy Colls led non‑invasive surveys (including lidar and geophysical methods) beginning in 2007 and followed with limited test excavations that revealed remains and structural traces the Nazis had tried to erase.

Key findings
- Lidar revealed previously unknown depressions indicating mass graves, particularly in Treblinka I (the labor camp). Test trenches exposed shoes, ammunition, human bones — some with cut marks — confirming killings there as well as in the better‑known death camp area.
- Excavations at Treblinka II (the extermination camp) uncovered brick foundations and wall fragments from gas chambers, orange floor tiles stamped with Stars of David matching survivor descriptions, and human bone fragments. These corroborate eyewitness accounts that victims were told they were entering bathhouses and were gassed with engine exhaust.
- Evidence showed the Nazis attempted to disguise and destroy the camp—dumping quarry sand and razing buildings and graves—but could not fully eliminate physical traces. Some bone fragments are already eroding to the forest surface.

Method and ethics
- Colls prioritized non‑invasive techniques and conducted only small, carefully controlled trenches to confirm subsurface features. Finds were treated with reverence: excavated human remains were reburied under rabbinical supervision in keeping with Jewish law.

Significance
- The work provides the first archaeological confirmation at Treblinka of gas chambers and additional mass graves, strengthening the documentary and testimonial record against denial. Colls plans further targeted investigations, museum displays, and a book to preserve and explain the evidence. The project aims both to document the historical truth and to help prevent future genocides.

The documentary premieres March 29 on the Smithsonian Channel; the research is ongoing and intended for respectful public presentation and scholarly record.

Sen. Charles Schumer urged bipartisan action and a full congressional investigation after the CIA told key senators in a classified briefing that it now assesses Russia intervened in the 2016 U.S. presidential election with the goal of helping Donald Trump win. The CIA’s assessment, reportedly based on multiple sources and identifying individuals tied to the Russian government who passed hacked Democratic emails to WikiLeaks, marks a shift from earlier public intelligence statements that focused on undermining confidence in the electoral process rather than favoring a candidate.

Schumer called the findings both “stunning and not surprising,” demanded the intelligence community turn over relevant material, and said Democrats would work with Republicans next year to hold hearings. The CIA’s presentation to senators indicated cyber-intrusions affected at least two states and that two Russian-linked hacker groups—commonly labelled “Cozy Bear” (APT29) and “Fancy Bear” (APT28/G.R.U.)—were involved; some stolen materials were published by outlets such as Guccifer 2.0, DCLeaks and WikiLeaks.

The Trump transition team and President-elect Trump publicly disputed the CIA’s conclusions; WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange denied Russia was the source. Within government, officials debated how to respond: the Obama White House ordered a “lessons learned” review to be completed before the January transition and sought bipartisan support earlier to publicly blame Russia and offer federal help to protect state election systems. Some Republican lawmakers expressed skepticism about the evidence. Critics say the administration was overly cautious and could have used sanctions or covert responses earlier. The episode has prompted calls from Democrats in Congress for declassification and broader investigations into the scope and motivations of the Russian campaign.

Three preschoolers in Honolulu were briefly exposed to a household cleaner after an aide accidentally served Pine‑Sol instead of apple juice at Kilohana United Methodist Church Preschool. The aide retrieved a yellow/brown liquid container from a cleanup cart in the kitchen, returned to the classroom with crackers and the container, and poured the liquid into cups while the lead teacher attended to students. The teacher stopped the children once she noticed the smell; three children ages 4 and 5 had taken small sips and were evaluated by paramedics, who found no signs of illness or injury. Parents declined hospital transport. The Pine‑Sol remained in its original, properly labeled container and cleaning supplies were stored separately from food; health inspectors reviewed the site after the incident and the school passed inspection. The classroom assistant no longer works at the preschool. Parents were notified by email and invited to a meeting; some remain unsettled though officials say precautions and food‑safety storage were in place.

Toronto police have officially reclassified the Dec. 15 deaths of billionaire Apotex founder Barry Sherman, 75, and his wife Honey, 70, as a targeted double homicide after six weeks of investigation, Det.-Sgt. Susan Gomes said at a news briefing. Both were found in the couple’s north Toronto home’s lower-level pool area, fully clothed with belts around their necks attached to a pool railing; post-mortems gave cause of death as ligature neck compression but initially left manner undetermined.

Investigators have pursued an extensive probe: roughly 2,000 hours of nearby surveillance footage collected, more than 150 items seized from the scene, about 127 witness interviews, execution or application for some 20 judicial authorizations/searches, searches of two Sherman residences (including a Miami condo) and of Barry Sherman’s Apotex workplace. Gomes said legal complexities—particularly around seizing electronics tied to Sherman's litigious businesses—made some warrants challenging. Police also compiled a list of everyone who accessed the house via the realtor’s lock box while it was listed for sale; that list has broadened the pool of persons of interest they plan to interview. To date, detectives say they have not developed any suspects and will not discuss motives.

Gomes emphasized that investigators considered all possibilities from the start (double suicide, homicide-suicide, double homicide) and have followed the evidence. The Shermans’ family, who earlier hired a private team of former homicide detectives after disputing early media leaks of a murder-suicide theory, supports the police conclusion and continues to cooperate. The house has been released back to the family, and the investigation remains active as police urge anyone with information to come forward.

Donald Trump announced his campaign will skip the Fox News Republican debate scheduled for Thursday in Des Moines, citing what he and his team called unfair treatment by Fox anchor Megyn Kelly. Campaign manager Corey Lewandowski confirmed the decision and said Trump will instead hold a simultaneous Iowa event to raise money for Wounded Warriors and veterans. The move came after a weeklong spat with Fox, including a sarcastic Fox statement ridiculing Trump and the campaign alleging Kelly had treated him unfairly after an earlier debate.

Fox News and CEO Roger Ailes pushed back, saying the network and Kelly will not be dictated to by a candidate and condemning what it described as threats toward Kelly from Trump’s camp; Fox insisted the debate will proceed with or without Trump. Trump’s campaign framed the walkout as principled bargaining—refusing a “bad deal” and accusing Fox of profiting heavily from debates—while Trump argued he would dominate the news cycle and raise funds for veterans.

Rival candidates and commentators reacted sharply: Ted Cruz called Trump “afraid” to face questions; Chris Christie and others said skipping a debate looks unpresidential and raises questions about temperament. Some supporters viewed the move as savvy showmanship that would keep Trump in headlines and undermine the debate’s impact. The decision comes days before the Iowa caucuses, where polls showed Trump leading, and leaves the remaining candidates to decide whether to use the debate to press advantages or avoid amplifying Trump’s absence. Fox warned Iowans might resent his last-minute withdrawal, and the standoff left open the possibility of last-minute negotiations, though Trump’s campaign signaled he was unlikely to change course.

A powerful, shallow magnitude ~6–6.2 earthquake struck central Italy in the pre-dawn hours of Aug. 24, 2016, near towns including Amatrice, Accumoli and Pescara del Tronto. The temblor devastated medieval town centers of unreinforced masonry, collapsing buildings onto sleeping residents and producing apocalyptic scenes of rubble, dust and gas smells. Hundreds of aftershocks followed. Initial reports gave rising death tolls (from dozens to well over 200), hundreds injured and many missing; thousands of residents, including summer visitors, needed temporary shelter.

Massive rescue efforts involving the army, Alpine units, carabinieri, firefighters, Red Cross and volunteers used bulldozers, earthmovers, sniffer dogs and hand digging to free survivors, but described equipment and personnel shortages in some hamlets. Authorities requested satellite imagery and appeals were made for blood donations and specialized tools. Italian leaders including Prime Minister Matteo Renzi visited the area and vowed support; Pope Francis led prayers and sent Vatican firefighters.

Seismologists noted the quake’s destructiveness was exacerbated by its shallow depth and the prevalence of ancient, unreinforced stone buildings that are difficult and expensive to retrofit. The quake occurred in a tectonically complex area where the Tyrrhenian Basin is spreading and multiple faults run along the Apennines; such shallow normal-fault earthquakes are common in central Italy and comparable to the 2009 L’Aquila disaster. Experts stressed that while Italy has strong codes for new construction, vulnerability remains high because of historic buildings and dense settlement, and that significant aftershocks can be expected.

Two pieces look at competing signals about the 2014 midterms and why modelers favor Republicans while some polling and on-the-ground factors give Democrats reason for cautious optimism.

Key points favoring Republicans
- Several respected forecasters and models (Cook Political Report, FiveThirtyEight, Upshot, Monkey Cage and others) have moved toward projecting a Republican Senate takeover. Nate Silver’s model gives Republicans roughly a 60% chance; the Monkey Cage model is even more bullish.
- Structural factors that historically predict midterm losses for the president’s party are present: sixth year of the presidential term, tepid presidential approval, poor “right/wrong track” metrics, and an unfavorable map.
- Republicans need a net gain of six Senate seats. Three states (Montana, South Dakota, West Virginia) are very likely to flip. If they pick up a few more — by winning open or vulnerable seats in red or purple states — they can take control.
- Several Republican pickup opportunities exist in red-leaning or Obama-lost states; incumbents in Alaska, Arkansas, Louisiana and North Carolina are the most plausible Democratic losses (Arkansas and Louisiana look best for GOP). Additional targets include competitive or potentially competitive Obama states such as Colorado, Iowa, Michigan, New Hampshire, and a second tier including Minnesota, Oregon and Virginia.

Reasons for Democratic hope and reasons to be cautious about the models
- Party image and identity advantage: ABC/Washington Post polling shows Democrats with far higher party favorability (49% vs. 35%) and larger self-identified party ID (32% Democrats vs. 22% Republicans). Those are historically large gaps and could blunt a GOP wave.
- Candidate quality and incumbency: Democrats point to stronger-than-expected candidates in many races, weak GOP challengers in some key states, and the difficulty of persuading voters about already heavily attacked incumbents like Kay Hagan and Mark Pryor.
- Ground game and turnout: Democrats say they are investing heavily in voter ID, registration and turnout operations that could mitigate structural disadvantages; whether that effort will succeed won’t be clear until Election Day.
- Intangibles: Outcomes still depend on evolving local dynamics, campaign performance, national mood, Obama’s standing, voter enthusiasm (currently favoring Republicans), and advertising/money.

Bottom line
Professional forecasters reasonably see the Senate leaning Republican given historical patterns and the map, but significant uncertainties remain. Party favorability, candidate quality, Democratic turnout operations, and state-level campaign dynamics mean a GOP takeover is plausible but not guaranteed; control will be decided state by state in the coming months.

British police are preparing to begin new excavations in Portugal as part of the long-running inquiry into Madeleine McCann’s disappearance in May 2007, reports say. Operation Grange investigators plan to travel to the Praia da Luz area to carry out ground searches at three sites, including two plots near the Ocean Club apartment (5A) where Madeleine vanished and a nearby beach area. A forensic team is expected to use ground-penetrating radar and other equipment to probe beneath the surface; Portuguese authorities will remain in charge of the criminal investigation.

Scotland Yard has not publicly confirmed the operation, saying it will not comment on speculation, but sources say the McCanns have been briefed and will be kept informed though they will not travel to Portugal. Officers say the digs aim both to seek potential evidence and to rule scenarios in or out; the family have been told this does not necessarily mean police are specifically searching for a body.

The renewed activity follows a wider review by the Met (Operation Grange), which began in 2011 and became a formal investigation in 2013, and new information that came in after recent appeals (including a Crimewatch broadcast). The Met has also been investigating a possible serial sex offender linked to multiple assaults on British girls in Algarve resorts between 2004 and 2010. Portuguese detectives reopened aspects of their probe last year and the British team hopes to work on the ground in coordination with them. A £20,000 reward remains available for information leading to arrest and prosecution.

Comedian Seth Rogen and his mother, Sandy Rogen, exchanged humorous tweets after Sandy posted a blunt observation about sex. On July 5, 2017, Sandy tweeted, “Falling asleep after sex is like shavasana after yoga.!” Her tweet was widely retweeted, prompting followers to tag Seth. He replied, “Jesus fucking Christ mom,” which sparked a playful back-and-forth: Sandy defended it as “just an observation of life,” Seth called it “gnarly,” and Sandy responded with teasing “Whateverrrrrrrr mom mm!” She later tweeted “Lame!” The exchange drew amusement online as a light, relatable parent-child moment on Twitter.

Edward Conard, a former Bain Capital partner and major Romney donor, argues in his book Unintended Consequences that the vast wealth of the superrich largely benefits the rest of society by financing innovation and risk-taking. Conard claims investors create far more public value than they capture—he rejects the common progressive estimate that each dollar earned by investors yields about $5 of public benefit and instead suggests returns could be as high as $20 per dollar. Using examples from tech and agricultural efficiency to tiny manufacturing improvements, he stresses that wealthy investors fund many of the incremental gains that cumulatively make consumers richer.

Conard defends complex financial institutions and instruments, portraying banks as intermediaries that convert short-term savings into long-term investment and arguing the 2008 crisis reflected a classic bank run by panicked institutional withdrawers rather than systemic fraud or irresponsible lending. He favors stronger government guarantees to prevent future runs and sees exotic securities as legitimate tools that met market demand.

Philosophically, Conard contends that higher rewards for success are necessary to entice more people to take risky, high-value bets; he even argues the top of the wealth distribution should be larger to motivate “art-history majors” and others to join the high-risk, high-reward innovation economy. He views U.S. policy choices and cultural accidents as key to American dynamism and warns that policies aimed at reducing inequality could dampen incentives to invest.

Critics—progressive economists, and many mainstream scholars—challenge Conard’s optimism about markets, financial products, and inequality. They point to rent-seeking, political influence by the wealthy, evidence of abusive banking practices before 2008, and research suggesting concentrated wealth can stifle innovation rather than promote it. Even some pro-market economists accept parts of his finance analysis but fault his dismissal of crony capitalism and his broad faith that market rewards reliably correspond to social value.

The profile portrays Conard as unapologetically pro-investor, relying on anecdotes, economic intuition, and mathematical reasoning to justify controversial positions that invert common critiques of rising inequality: for him, concentrated wealth is, on balance, a public good.

- A CBRE study finds Denver’s cannabis industry now occupies roughly 3.7 million (CBRE) to about 4.5 million (later correction) square feet of industrial space — about one in 11 industrial buildings and roughly 2.6% of all warehouse space in the city. Grow operations are concentrated in older, lower-quality warehouse areas (I‑25/I‑70 junction, Montbello, Central Denver, Santa Fe Drive corridor and RiNo).

- From 2009–2014 marijuana cultivation accounted for 35.8% of industrial leases in Denver, helping spur the recovery of the industrial market from the Great Recession. That demand has contributed to rising rents and falling vacancy: metro industrial rents reached about $7.05/sq ft in Q3, Class B/C rents in cultivation neighborhoods rose 56% over five years, and vacancy in many grow-heavy submarkets is very low (North Central 1.9%, Central 2.3%, Southwest 2.4%).

- Marijuana tenants often pay significant rent premiums (commonly 2–3× market rates) and typically lease 10,000–20,000 sq ft (range 2,000–100,000). Many owners won’t lease to growers because of federal legality issues, lender restrictions, and the cost of required electrical/HVAC upgrades; landlords willing to assume risk are a small group.

- CBRE calls the market “overgrown”: some grow space remains vacant and many existing operations aren’t at capacity, so immediate additional demand may be limited unless Denver lifts a recreational-license moratorium (affecting applicants established before Oct. 1, 2013), which could spur more entrants.

- Broader effects: growers have bid up prices for marginal industrial properties that previously housed artists and small creative enterprises (notably in RiNo), displacing cultural uses and potentially delaying redevelopment because long-term grow leases lock in aging buildings. Critics argue the cannabis boom contributes to displacement, higher housing costs and homelessness pressures, although other forces (in-migration of higher-paid workers, condo-law impacts on supply) are also important drivers of Denver’s affordability crisis.

- The industry’s rapid growth has not been matched by comprehensive academic or governmental study of long-term impacts; stakeholders call for more research on how retail and cultivation cannabis reshape real estate, neighborhoods and local economy.

This document is a compilation of several critics’ takes on the 2015 comedy Sisters, starring Tina Fey and Amy Poehler as Kate and Maura Ellis — two estranged thirty-/forty-something sisters who reunite to clean out their childhood home in Orlando and instead throw a massive, increasingly out-of-control party. The movie, written by Paula Pell and directed by Jason Moore, leans heavily on raunchy, R-rated humor, gross-out set pieces and extended slapstick, and features a large supporting cast of comedic familiar faces (Ike Barinholtz, Maya Rudolph, John Leguizamo, Bobby Moynihan, Rachel Dratch, John Cena, Samantha Bee, and others).

Common points across the reviews:
- Fey and Poehler’s chemistry is the film’s primary asset. Their rapport, timing and likability make many crude or silly moments work, and they convincingly play competitive-but-loving sisters: Poehler’s Maura as the anxious do-gooder and Fey’s Kate as the irresponsible wild child.
- The movie is structured largely around the blowout party, which escalates into sex- and drug-fueled chaos and provides the bulk of the film’s comic set pieces and cameos.
- Critics are divided on tone and quality. Some praise the film as a loose, infectious, good-time comedy that showcases the duo’s strengths and yields genuinely funny bits and warm character moments. The quieter, character-driven scenes and some visual gags are highlighted as memorable.
- Many reviewers fault the film for thin plotting, sloppy direction, uneven writing, and wasted supporting talent. Several argue the vulgarity and crude gags often come off as gratuitous rather than clever, and that secondary characters and recurring bits frequently fall flat. Some say the movie resembles an “Animal House”-style frat/party movie filtered through female leads, but without the discipline to make it consistently satisfying.
- Opinions on whether the raunch pays off vary: proponents find it an entertaining, convivial romp that’s better than its trailers; detractors call it badly directed and written, arguing it’s bad for big-screen comedy when actors of this caliber are underutilized in such a muddled product.

Overall, Sisters is portrayed as a film buoyed by Fey and Poehler’s charm and comic partnership but hampered by uneven comedy, sketchy plotting, and overreliance on vulgar set pieces — fun in spots but flawed and divisive in execution.

A 3-acre Deerfield Beach parcel at Southeast Fourth Street and Second Avenue, long known as the "old colored cemetery," may be rezoned for a 69-unit townhouse development called Village Park at Deerfield Beach. The proposal will be debated by the City Commission at a special meeting after months of controversy that stretch back four decades.

Background: Historical records and local testimony say the site was used as an African American cemetery from roughly the late 19th century through the 1930s–1940s, with some estimates of 300–400 interments. The site was cleared of headstones in the 1970s amid earlier development attempts that were stopped by community protest. Residents continue to say relatives were buried there and that they saw burials.

Investigations: Two major studies—one by Florida Atlantic University anthropologists in 1986 using magnetometer searches and shovel tests, and another in 2005 involving ground-penetrating radar and overseen by local historical societies—found no physical evidence of burials remaining on the site. The 2005 work concluded at least 34 bodies had been moved to the city-owned Pineview Cemetery in 1974; city officials, including Mayor Jean Robb, suspect additional remains were relocated in the 1960s because of a high water table, but cannot confirm specifics from records.

Positions: City officials and the property owner’s representatives argue the site is clear of remains and that development would improve tax revenue and neighborhood value. Many longtime residents and descendants of those believed buried there oppose construction on moral and cultural grounds, demand proof of where any remains were moved, and warn of the emotional harm and disrespect of building on cemetery land.

Next steps: Commissioners delayed final approval to review staff reports and documentation about whether remains remain on the property; they scheduled further discussion and possible rezoning votes at a special meeting. The unresolved question—where the bodies went—remains a central grievance for descendants despite the studies’ findings.

Seaman James Derek Lovelace, 21, of Crestview, Florida, died Friday during his first week of Basic Underwater Demolition/SEAL (BUD/S) training at Naval Amphibious Base Coronado. During a pool familiarization or "drown‑proofing" evolution—treading and swimming while wearing dive masks and camouflage uniforms—safety observers saw Lovelace struggling. Instructors removed him to the pool edge after he lost consciousness; resuscitation on scene and at a nearby civilian hospital were unsuccessful and he was pronounced dead.

Naval Special Warfare Command has opened an investigation and local authorities will perform an autopsy; officials have not disclosed a cause of death or whether he had an underlying medical issue. Lovelace had enlisted in November, graduated Navy boot camp in January, and had been awarded the National Defense Service Ribbon and Sharpshooter Pistol Qualification. He played baseball at Crestview High School and Faulkner State Community College and is survived by his father and two sisters. Naval leaders expressed condolences and said training safety procedures include scaling instructor oversight when students show difficulty.

An Army wife, Amy Herbst, and her husband sued the government Monday, alleging a nurse-midwife at Blanchfield Army Community Hospital (Fort Campbell, Ky.) botched her 2012 childbirth and severely damaged her digestive and reproductive systems. The suit says the midwife performed an episiotomy during the second stage of labor without Herbst’s consent or knowledge and repaired it with sutures. After discharge, Herbst experienced fecal urgency, incontinence, stool leakage and excessive flatulence; hospital staff later told her initial repairs were unsuccessful and a colorectal surgeon said reconstructive surgery would be needed. Herbst says the injuries and poor prognosis have jeopardized her career as a professional opera singer with the Nashville Opera Company. The hospital declined to comment on the specific case but said it is concerned about patient outcomes and strives to provide high-quality care.

The White House has, for the first time in an unclassified document, formally acknowledged that U.S. military forces have conducted “direct action” — a military term encompassing lethal attacks — against al-Qaida affiliates in Yemen and Somalia. The admission appears in the semiannual War Powers report to Congress and marks a modest step toward transparency about U.S. counterterror operations beyond Afghanistan and Pakistan.

The report states U.S. forces carried out a “limited number” of operations targeting al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) in Yemen and al-Shabaab–linked al-Qaida members in Somalia, emphasizing the focus on individuals who pose a direct threat to the United States and its interests. It does not provide operational details, mention specific tactics or platforms (such as armed drones), or disclose classified specifics, which are included in a secret annex provided to Congress.

Administration officials said President Obama approved the declassification of the existence of these military efforts partly because of closer ties with the Yemeni government and other partners concerned with Somali extremism. The move follows earlier, more general acknowledgments (e.g., John Brennan’s confirmation of armed drone use) but does not indicate any change in the intensity or nature of the campaign. The disclosure comes amid congressional scrutiny and controversy over leaks related to targeted-killing programs.

Summary:

After conceding the presidential race to Barack Obama, Mitt Romney’s official Facebook page experienced a rapid drop in likes — roughly 11 per minute (about 600–850 per hour), totaling more than 50,000–55,000 unlikes in the days after the election. A satirical site, DisappearingRomney.com, tracked the decline in real time. The Romney campaign’s social accounts went largely silent after Election Day, posting only a brief thank-you/photo, while President Obama’s profiles remained active and saw large gains. Romney still retained a large following (over 12 million Facebook likes and 1.7 million Twitter followers), and his Twitter account actually gained some followers despite no new tweets. The exodus may reflect both post-election disengagement, staff transitions that often accompany campaign endings, and partisan shifts as supporters look for new leaders; by contrast, some defeated politicians have later revived strong online presences, but Romney’s future public role remained uncertain.

A tenant in an Arlington, Virginia rental heard footsteps coming from her attic around 1:30 a.m. on July 21 and alerted her landlord, who called Arlington County Police. Officers searched the home on the 800 block of 22nd Street S. near Pentagon City and found 60-year-old Anthony Jones living in the attic with a backpack, clothing and bedding. Jones, believed to have entered through an open sliding glass door, came down when officers announced their presence and was arrested without incident and charged with unlawful entry; he was being held without bail. The tenant said the quick police response made her feel safer. The report also notes other recent Arlington incidents, including a strong-armed robbery on Washington Boulevard and several larcenies, shoplifting, destruction of property reports and a stolen 2004 Dodge Caravan.

Actors Michael Douglas and Catherine Zeta-Jones are reportedly taking time apart after more than two decades of marriage. People magazine, citing unnamed sources, says the couple — married in 2000 and parents of two (Dylan, 13, and Carys, 10) — have been spending time separately since Douglas returned from the Cannes Film Festival in May. They have not filed for divorce or legal separation. Friends and confidantes tell PEOPLE the strain from Douglas’s 2010 cancer battle and Zeta-Jones’s struggles with bipolar II disorder contributed to the decision, though those close to them hope they can work things out for the children’s sake. Zeta-Jones’s spokeswoman, Cece Yorke, confirmed in an email to the Associated Press that they are “taking some time apart to evaluate and work on their marriage” and declined further comment; a representative for Douglas did not immediately respond.

Blind civil-rights activist Chen Guangcheng, who escaped prolonged house arrest in rural Shandong and briefly sheltered at the U.S. Embassy in Beijing, has demanded that China’s central government investigate and punish local Shandong officials he blames for his wrongful jailing, abuse and 19 months of punitive confinement. Speaking from a Beijing hospital where he is being treated for injuries sustained during his escape and years of mistreatment, Chen said he intends to continue “rights defence” work and pressed Beijing to probe specific officials, including Linyi public security chief Liu Jie and former Linyi party boss Li Qun.

Under a fragile, U.S.-China arrangement, Chen said he hopes to travel to the United States to recuperate and study—New York University has offered him a fellowship—and he expressed cautious confidence that Beijing will honor the agreement allowing him to apply for travel documents. He reported meeting a central government official who promised an open legal inquiry “if the facts are there,” but said no concrete action had occurred yet.

Chen also said relatives in his home village of Dongshigu remain under pressure: his nephew Chen Kegui was reportedly detained after a violent confrontation with local officials, his brother has faced threats, and villagers and journalists have encountered lockdowns and guards. U.S. diplomats have been in regular phone contact with Chen but have been prevented from visiting him in person; Chinese authorities likewise limited his access to friends. The episode has triggered a diplomatic standoff and high-level U.S.-China engagement to resolve Chen’s case without derailing broader ties.

In 1963 teenagers Barbara Bezant (17) and Lyn Jeffries (19) recorded a reel-to-reel message for The Beatles after seeing them at the Lewisham Odeon and sent the tape to the Finsbury Park Astoria. Decades later the tape surfaced at a Great Yarmouth car boot sale, where historian David McDermott purchased and listened to it. The BBC’s The One Show tracked down and reunited the two women at The Beatles Story in Liverpool and presented them with a letter from Sir Paul McCartney, who thanked them for their “lovely tape,” quipped “better late than never,” and encouraged them to “keep enjoying the music.” The women, who had not seen each other for 40 years though both lived in Essex, said they were “amazed” to be reunited and to receive a reply from a Beatle.

The Trump administration signaled it might stay in the Paris climate agreement—or rejoin under revised terms—if its conditions are met, marking a shift from President Trump’s earlier announcement that the U.S. would withdraw if it couldn’t secure more favorable terms. At a Montreal meeting of over 30 ministers hosted by Canada, China and the EU, U.S. officials suggested they were open to revising U.S. emissions targets as part of a compromise. The discussions indicate Washington is exploring options to re-engage with the global deal while seeking adjustments to how commitments are framed or implemented.

President Trump attacked adult-film actress Stormy Daniels and her lawyer Michael Avenatti after a federal judge dismissed Daniels’ defamation suit against him, calling Daniels “horseface” in a tweet and saying he could “go after” her and her “3rd rate lawyer” in Texas. The judge found Trump’s tweet at issue was constitutionally protected speech and applied Texas law, dismissing the suit and ordering Daniels to pay Trump’s attorneys’ fees; Avenatti has appealed.

The exchange escalated: Avenatti called Trump “a disgusting misogynist” and vowed to expose him as a “shyster and liar,” while Daniels replied to Trump by criticizing him and nicknaming him “Tiny.” Trump defended his insult when questioned.

The incident renewed concerns among Republicans about alienating female voters ahead of the midterms. The story notes a pattern of Trump mocking women’s appearances—including Christine Blasey Ford, Elizabeth Warren and others—which has alarmed some GOP allies and may be contributing to shifting support among women, particularly college-educated white women, toward Democrats. The piece also references Daniels’ separate legal challenge to a nondisclosure agreement tied to a $130,000 payment from Michael Cohen and reviews public reactions and polling showing the political sensitivity of such comments.

An Upper East Side auction house, Doyle New York, sold a newly consigned group of love letters John F. Kennedy wrote to Swedish socialite Gunilla von Post for an estimated $10,000–$15,000. The correspondence, discovered among von Post’s belongings after her 2011 death and dated 1954–1956, includes two complete signed letters on Senate stationery, two partial letters and three handwritten envelopes, and comes with von Post’s 1997 memoir Love, Jack. A previous cache of their letters fetched $115,000 in 2010; together the two lots constitute the known corpus of their exchanges.

Von Post met the young senator in Cannes in 1953; the letters chronicle a long-distance, often passionate affair that continued after Kennedy’s 1953 marriage to Jackie. Early notes show Kennedy attempting to meet her in Stockholm (a 1954 visit was canceled for back surgery) and later arranging a 1955 rendezvous in Båstad, writing, “It is a long way to Gunilla — it is worth it.” Von Post’s memoir recounts that they reunited in August 1955 and spent a week together in Sweden, after which Kennedy reportedly contemplated ending his marriage and bringing her to America. Political pressures, his father, and sensitivities around Jackie’s miscarriage (1955) and pregnancy (1956) prevented that. Kennedy’s final letter to von Post, written after she announced plans to marry a Swedish landowner, urged her to come visit if she did not marry and closed, “I had a wonderful time last summer with you. It is a bright memory of my life — you are wonderful and I miss you.” The two met once more, accidentally, at a Waldorf Astoria gala in 1958.

The article also contextualizes Jackie Kennedy’s difficult reproductive history—miscarriage in 1955, a stillbirth in 1956, the birth of Caroline in 1957, and the birth and 1963 death of infant Patrick—noting how these events affected the Kennedys’ marriage and JFK’s public image during his political rise.

Overview:
In early March 2016, former Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney delivered a forceful, high-profile speech at the University of Utah sharply criticizing Donald Trump’s candidacy and arguing that Trump is unfit to be the Republican nominee. The speech intensified an intra‑party fight as establishment Republicans sought to slow Trump’s momentum after his string of primary victories.

Key points from Romney’s speech:
- Romney repeatedly attacked Trump’s character and competence, calling him “a phony, a fraud” and saying “dishonesty is Donald Trump’s hallmark.”
- He criticized Trump’s rhetoric (bullying, misogyny, vulgarity) and cited numerous episodes—mocking a disabled reporter, derogatory comments about women, inflammatory comments about Muslims and Mexicans, and praise of sexual exploits—as evidence Trump is unfit for office.
- Romney condemned Trump’s foreign-policy proposals—calling Trump “very, very not-smart” for suggesting letting ISIS remove Assad and for advocating extreme measures such as killing terrorists’ families—and warned such ideas are reckless and dangerous.
- He argued Trump’s trade and economic proposals (tariffs, tax plans) would provoke trade wars, raise the deficit, harm workers and could precipitate a prolonged recession.
- Romney warned of the long-term damage to the Republican Party and the country if Trump became the nominee, urging voters to back any alternative who could beat Hillary Clinton in the general election.

Political posture and endorsements:
- Romney did not enter the 2016 race or endorse a single candidate outright. Instead he said he would support Marco Rubio in Florida or John Kasich in Ohio (reflecting state-by-state preferences) and named Rubio, Ted Cruz and John Kasich as acceptable alternatives, framing his remarks as an appeal to prevent a Trump coronation and to engineer a contested convention if necessary.
- He invoked his status as a party elder and urged conservatives to coalesce behind someone else to preserve conservative values and electability.

Reactions and context:
- Donald Trump immediately lauded his own appeal to new voters and attacked Romney on social media, calling him a “failed presidential candidate” and mocking Romney’s 2012 bid and prior courting of Trump’s endorsement.
- Trump supporters circulated clips of Romney praising Trump in 2012 to underscore Romney’s reversal.
- Prominent Republicans were split: figures such as John McCain publicly agreed with Romney’s concerns about Trump’s national-security statements, while others (including some conservative activists and Trump allies) defended Trump and cautioned against giving him more attention.
- The speech reflected broader Republican establishment efforts—including super PAC ads—to derail Trump’s momentum, but commentators noted Romney might have limited effect given Trump’s strong primary performance and devoted base.

Public reaction and significance:
- Romney drew large crowds and applause in Utah, where many attendees expressed concern about Trump; some wished Romney would run again.
- Still, many voters who prioritized defeating Democrats or were energized by Trump’s outsider message indicated they might back Trump despite Romney’s criticisms.
- The episode underscored deep tensions within the GOP between the traditional establishment and the insurgent populist movement driving Trump’s rise.

Bottom line:
Romney’s March 2016 speech was a comprehensive, personal and policy-focused rebuke of Donald Trump—framing Trump as dishonest, reckless on foreign policy, economically harmful and unfit for the presidency—and was part of a broader, albeit uncertain, establishment effort to stop Trump’s nomination.

Serena Williams and fiancé Alexis Ohanian have welcomed their first child, a baby girl, on Friday, September 1, 2017. Multiple outlets report the newborn weighed 6 pounds, 13 ounces and that both mother and baby are doing well. Williams, 35, announced her pregnancy earlier this year—initially via an accidental Snapchat post in April—while she had already won the Australian Open in January. She documented parts of her pregnancy publicly, appeared on Vanity Fair’s August cover, and said she planned to return to professional tennis (aiming for the Australian Open). Beyoncé was among the first to congratulate her, and family and fans reacted warmly, including sister Venus at the U.S. Open. Williams and Ohanian, co‑founder of Reddit, became engaged in December 2016; they have not yet announced a wedding date.

A humorous Craigslist ad for a 1999 Toyota Corolla, shared on Twitter by Brendan Tokarski, went viral for its blunt honesty and entertaining tone. The seller leans into the car’s plainness—no Bluetooth, sunroof, fancy wheels, or rear camera—but markets it as extremely reliable, joking it could survive being driven off a bridge, run on Nutella, and outlive its owner. The listing mixes practical claims ("It’s a Corolla. It’s fine." per a CarFax) with surreal, comic details (favorite food: spaghetti; favorite TV show: Alf; likes Bush and the Gin Blossoms) and offbeat lines about the car being old enough to vote. Readers appreciated the ode to the Corolla’s reputation for durability, even if it’s boring, and the ad has since been removed—possibly because it sold or because the seller couldn’t part with the car.

Summary:

A three-man crew dubbed the "Cold Hand Bandits" has robbed about 23–24 banks across the Los Angeles area since November 2015. LAPD’s Robbery-Homicide Division, working with the FBI and multiple local agencies (Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department, Alhambra, Pasadena and Long Beach police), released surveillance footage and appealed to the public for help identifying the suspects, who remain at large and are considered armed and dangerous.

Modus operandi and behavior:
- The suspects typically walk into banks and hand tellers a note demanding money, claiming to be armed and threatening violence if refused.
- Their tactics have become more aggressive: in recent incidents they have jumped over teller counters, one suspect brandished what appeared to be a gun, and another used his shirt to avoid leaving fingerprints.
- No injuries have been reported so far, but police worry the threats could turn violent.

Descriptions:
- Three Black men, roughly 25–30 years old.
- Two are about 5'7"–5'9" and 170–190 lbs; the third about 5'6"–5'7" and 140–160 lbs.
- One early robber was seen wearing winter gloves, giving rise to the “Cold Hand” nickname.

Investigators urge anyone with information to contact the LAPD Robbery-Homicide Division or Crime Stoppers; tip lines and anonymous reporting options were provided. Police stress urgency because of the frequency and escalating brazenness of the robberies.

Superstorm Sandy battered the U.S. East Coast at the end of October, leaving widespread death, destruction and major disruptions across multiple states. By Tuesday the confirmed U.S. death toll was in the 40s (reports varied around 46), with many fatalities from falling trees, flooding or storm-related accidents; the storm had already killed dozens in the Caribbean before making landfall in New Jersey Monday evening.

Scope and human impact
- Coastal surges up to about 13–14 feet inundated low-lying areas; Lower Manhattan set a record tide of 13.88 feet.
- Entire neighborhoods were flooded or leveled, including massive fires in Breezy Point, Queens, that destroyed scores of homes.
- Hospitals were evacuated after power failures; many residents were stranded or forced from homes, and rescues were ongoing in hard-hit communities (e.g., Moonachie, NJ; Atlantic City; parts of Long Island and northern New Jersey).
- Authorities described the damage as unprecedented in a generation and “incalculable.”

Infrastructure, services and economics
- More than 6.6–8.2 million customers lost power across the region (most in New York and New Jersey).
- New York’s subway system suffered catastrophic flooding (stations and tunnels inundated, some up to ceiling level), with full service expected to be down several days; PATH and other commuter lines faced multi-day suspensions.
- Major airports in the region were closed (JFK, LaGuardia, Newark among others); over 16,000–18,000 flights were canceled nationally during the event, and stock exchanges were closed for weather-related reasons for the first time since 1888.
- Levees breached in parts of northern New Jersey, submerging towns; boardwalks and piers were washed away along the Jersey Shore and Atlantic City.
- Initial insured-loss estimates ran from billions (AIR Worldwide: $7–15 billion); some forecasts placed total property damage and economic losses in the tens of billions.

Geography and weather effects
- Sandy affected more than a half-dozen U.S. states from New England to the Midwest and Southeast. It merged with a cold front, creating a massive hybrid system that produced blizzard conditions and record October snows in parts of Appalachia, heavy rains and high winds across a broad area, and dangerous surf along the Great Lakes and Atlantic coasts.
- Canada (Ontario and Quebec) also experienced outages and at least one storm-related death.

Government response
- President Obama declared major disasters in New York, New Jersey and Connecticut, pledged federal resources, and planned visits to affected areas. Governors and local officials reported extensive damage and mobilized rescues and recovery operations; the National Guard and FEMA were being deployed.
- Officials warned recovery would take time and emphasized public safety—urging people to avoid parks, downed lines and flooded streets.

Overall picture
Sandy was a historic, complex storm whose storm surge, winds and flooding caused concentrated devastation across densely populated coastal areas—paralyzing mass transit, cutting power to millions, destroying homes and infrastructure, and producing heavy economic losses. Recovery and restoration of services were expected to be slow and costly.

Researchers have identified bovine belching—enteric fermentation in ruminants—as a major source of anthropogenic methane, a potent short-term greenhouse gas. Globally, livestock account for about 44% of human-caused methane from the food system; in the U.S., enteric fermentation contributes roughly 25–26% of methane emissions. Methane production in the rumen also represents lost feed energy for growth or milk.

A collaborative study led by Alexander Hristov (Penn State) with support from DSM tested the methane inhibitor 3‑nitrooxypropanol (3NOP) in a 12‑week randomized trial of 48 lactating Holstein cows. Cows received varying doses of 3NOP mixed into feed and methane was measured using feeding chambers and nostril-cannula methods. Key findings:
- 3NOP reduced enteric methane emissions by about 30% under industry-relevant conditions.
- Methane per unit of feed intake and per unit of energy-corrected milk fell by ~30%.
- Feed intake, milk production and fiber digestibility were not negatively affected; milk protein and lactose yields rose.
- Cows given 3NOP gained significantly more body weight (about 80% higher gain during the trial), indicating captured energy was redirected to tissue synthesis.
- The inhibitory effect persisted over the 12‑week period.

Independent experts welcomed the result but urged further work on the inhibitor’s mode of action, long‑term animal health effects, residues in manure/soil, environmental toxicity, and multi‑season trials. DSM aims to commercialize the additive and suggests farmers might later earn carbon credits for using it.

Overall, 3NOP shows promise as a scalable mitigation tool to cut ruminant methane emissions and improve feed efficiency, but longer-term, broader-scale studies and safety assessments are needed before widespread adoption.

Summary:

Steve Bannon stumped for Roy Moore in Fairhope, Alabama, primarily using the rally to attack national Republican figures—most notably Mitt Romney, Jeff Flake and Mitch McConnell—rather than focusing on Democrat Doug Jones. Bannon defended Moore, dismissed the sexual-misconduct allegations against him as a media “setup,” and promised to use Breitbart-style tactics that helped elect Donald Trump to secure Moore’s win. He also suggested he wants to keep Romney from running for the Utah Senate seat in 2018 and has even considered backing Orrin Hatch.

Bannon’s most personal attacks targeted Romney and his family, criticizing Romney’s Vietnam deferments and missionary service in France and mocking his sons’ lack of military service. Those attacks drew cheers from Moore supporters but provoked pushback from other Republicans: Senators Orrin Hatch and Mike Lee defended Romney’s missionary service, and Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell called Romney “truly remarkable” while deriding Bannon’s knack for backing losing candidates. Romney had publicly denounced Moore, calling him a “stain” on the GOP and praising Moore’s accusers as courageous; Jeff Flake even donated to Doug Jones.

Despite national Republican unease, Trump’s endorsement and renewed pro-Trump spending—which includes $1.1 million from a pro-Trump group and hundreds of thousands from Bannon-aligned groups—have revived Moore’s campaign, narrowing polls that showed him only slightly ahead of Democrat Doug Jones. Moore, who has largely stayed off TV and reduced public events since the allegations surfaced, portrayed himself at the rally as the victim of “fake news” and vowed to bring “Alabama values to Washington.”

The piece also notes the political calculus in Utah: Utah’s heavily Mormon electorate is generally hostile to Trump and sympathetic to Romney’s missionary service. Bannon’s attacks on Romney could therefore make any Bannon endorsement toxic in Utah and complicate Republican efforts there if Bannon intervenes in the 2018 Senate race. Overall, the coverage highlights GOP divisions over Moore, the tensions between nationalist/populist forces led by Bannon and more traditional Republicans, and how those rifts are reshaping campaigns and party dynamics.

House Republicans on Dec. 4 passed the Executive Amnesty Prevention Act, a mostly symbolic rebuke of President Obama’s recent executive actions on immigration that would declare any administration attempt to exempt people from deportation “null and void.” The bill, sponsored by Rep. Ted Yoho, passed the House 219–197 but faces certain defeat in the Democratic-controlled Senate and an Obama veto.

Leadership framed the vote as a way to register Republican opposition while avoiding a repeat shutdown fight: Boehner’s two-part strategy pairs the symbolic House measure with a plan to pass an omnibus funding bill keeping most agencies funded through September 2015 but funding Homeland Security only through February, preserving a future opportunity to press the administration on immigration. Conservative hard-liners pushed instead to insert anti-executive-action language into must-pass spending bills; some threatened to oppose Boehner’s funding plan as insufficiently aggressive. Boehner and other leaders say they need Democratic votes to pass the spending package and are seeking a pragmatic path that averts another fiscal crisis.

Democrats, immigrant advocates and the White House denounced the Yoho bill as harmful to families and unnecessary—arguing the president’s actions are lawful and needed given congressional inaction—and emphasized Congress should pursue comprehensive reform. The vote exposed intra-GOP tensions (a handful of Republicans opposed or voted present) and highlighted Nancy Pelosi’s insistence that Democrats will only support funding bills that don’t include harsh policy riders. Overall, the House action signals Republican opposition but is unlikely to change policy before the new Congress takes control.

A Chilean judge is continuing to probe the 1973 death of Nobel laureate Pablo Neruda and has ordered additional forensic tests on his remains. Judge Mario Carroza requested analyses for substances not examined in the initial investigation; those tests will be performed in Spain and other unspecified countries. Neruda’s body was exhumed in April 2013; earlier bone testing found no suspicious chemical agents, but his family and former driver—who has long alleged that dictatorship agents injected poison into the bedridden poet—asked for more proof. Officially Neruda, who suffered prostate cancer, died of natural causes on Sept. 23, 1973, soon after the Pinochet coup, but suspicions of foul play have persisted.

Separately, over 20 unpublished Neruda poems were discovered in boxes of his manuscripts at the Pablo Neruda Foundation in Chile. Described by his Spanish publisher Seix Barral and scholars as works of “extraordinary quality,” the poems—mostly love pieces and odes to everyday objects written after Canto General—will be published in Latin America in late 2014 and in Spain in early 2015. Biographers and critics praised the find but noted that definitive conclusions about Neruda’s death may remain difficult after four decades.

President Trump stopped in Warsaw on July 6 on his way to the G20 in Hamburg, meeting President Andrzej Duda and delivering a high-profile speech at the Three Seas Summit and in Krasinski Square. Poland’s conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS) views the visit as a diplomatic win, signaling U.S. goodwill for a government criticized at home and in Brussels for restricting judicial independence, attacking dissenting media, opposing migrant quotas and resisting EU climate rules.

Why Poland:
- A friendly reception: Poland’s ruling party organized large crowds and a favorable setting, ensuring positive optics unlike the protests expected at other stops.
- Ideological alignment: PiS and Trump share populist, nationalist stances—prioritizing national interests on immigration, climate policy and skepticism of liberal elites—making the visit mutually beneficial.
